note: Plain-English definitions of the terms a first-year gardener meets on seed packets, in extension guides and on this site. Each entry says what it means and why it matters, not just what it is.

terms.definition: A plant that completes its whole life — seed, growth, flower, seed again — in one season, then dies. Almost everything in a vegetable garden is an annual, which is why you sow again each year.
terms.why: It means an empty bed in autumn is normal, not a failure.

terms.definition: When a leafy or root crop suddenly shoots up a flower stalk and stops making the part you wanted to eat. Heat and lengthening days trigger it. Lettuce and spinach turn bitter once it happens.
terms.why: It is the single most common reason a spring crop of greens 'goes wrong' in June.

terms.definition: A crop that grows best in spring and autumn temperatures and tolerates some frost — peas, spinach, lettuce, radishes, kale, carrots, onions.
terms.why: These go in weeks before your last frost, and they are what you plant again in late summer for autumn.

terms.definition: The first one or two rounded leaves a seedling puts out. They came packed inside the seed and rarely look like the adult plant. The next pair are the 'true leaves'.
terms.why: Thinning and potting-on advice is usually keyed to true leaves, not these.

terms.definition: A fungal problem that makes healthy-looking seedlings collapse at the soil line overnight. Caused by soil that stays too wet with too little air movement.
terms.why: It is the main way indoor seed-starting fails, and it is prevented rather than cured.

terms.definition: The rough number of days from sowing until you can pick. For tomatoes and peppers it is counted from the day you transplant, not from seed — the seed packet will say which.
terms.why: It is how you work out whether a crop can finish before your first autumn frost.

terms.definition: Tomato growth habits. Determinate varieties grow to a set size and ripen most of their fruit at once. Indeterminate ones keep growing and keep fruiting until frost.
terms.why: Determinate suits containers and batch cooking; indeterminate suits a steady supply but needs real support.

terms.definition: Planting seed straight into the ground or container where it will grow, instead of starting it indoors and moving it.
terms.why: Fast crops and root crops nearly always do better this way — carrots especially resent being moved.

terms.definition: The average dates of the last freezing night in spring and the first in autumn. Every planting date in gardening is expressed relative to them.
terms.why: An 'average' date is where the chance of frost drops below 50 percent, so it is a coin flip, not a guarantee. Waiting a week past it is the safer read for tender crops.

terms.definition: How much cold a crop survives. Hardy crops go out as soon as the soil can be worked; half-hardy about 2 to 3 weeks before the last frost; tender crops only after it; very tender 2 to 3 weeks after.
terms.why: Getting this wrong is how a whole tray of seedlings dies in one night.

terms.definition: The moment a seed wakes up and sprouts. It depends far more on soil temperature and steady moisture than on the calendar.
terms.why: Cold soil is why seed 'never came up' — beans rot below 60°F, cucumbers and squash want 70°F.

terms.definition: Gradually introducing indoor-raised seedlings to outdoor sun, wind and cold over 7 to 10 days before planting them out.
terms.why: Skip it and indoor leaves scorch or wilt beyond recovery within a day or two. It is not optional.

terms.definition: A number from 3 to 10 describing your average coldest winter temperature. It is a winter-survival rating for perennials.
terms.why: It is not a frost-date band, even though nearly every gardening site treats it as one. Use it as a first guess, then get your real frost dates from a weather station near you.

terms.definition: A 2-inch layer of straw, shredded leaves or bark spread over the soil surface around plants, kept an inch clear of the stems.
terms.why: It holds moisture, suppresses most weeds and steadies soil temperature. The highest-value half hour in the whole garden.

terms.definition: A plant that lives for several years, dying back and returning each season. Asparagus, rhubarb and most herbs are perennial.
terms.why: Perennials need a permanent spot, so plan them at the edge of a bed where you will not dig them up.

terms.definition: How acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale where 7 is neutral. Most vegetables want 6.0 to 7.0.
terms.why: Well outside that range, plants cannot take up nutrients even when the nutrients are present — which looks like a feeding problem but is not.

terms.definition: Moving a seedling into a larger pot when its roots fill the one it is in, usually 3 to 4 weeks after sowing.
terms.why: A root-bound seedling stalls, and a stalled seedling is outperformed by one sown weeks later.

terms.term: Potting mix vs garden soil vs compost
terms.definition: Potting mix is a light, sterile blend for containers. Garden soil is what is in the ground. Compost is decomposed organic matter used to improve either.
terms.why: Garden soil compacts into a brick in a pot and drowns roots. Potting mix in a large raised bed is expensive and drains too fast. They are not interchangeable.

terms.definition: A finer, faster-draining, sterile mix made specifically for germinating seed indoors.
terms.why: It is the main defence against damping off, and unlike garden soil it carries no weed seeds or pathogens indoors.

terms.definition: Scattering a little fertiliser or compost along the row beside growing plants, mid-season, then watering it in.
terms.why: It feeds hungry crops like tomatoes and squash at the point they need it, without disturbing roots.

terms.definition: Sowing a short row of the same crop every couple of weeks instead of the whole packet at once.
terms.why: You get a steady supply rather than thirty radishes in one week. The easiest way to get more from a small bed.

terms.definition: Pulling out surplus seedlings so the ones left have their full spacing. Snip at soil level for crops that dislike root disturbance.
terms.why: It feels wasteful and beginners skip it. Crowded plants compete for light and water and all of them underperform.

terms.definition: As a verb, moving a young plant into its final position. As a noun, the young plant itself — also called a seedling, start or plug.
terms.why: 'Set out transplants after last frost' on a seed packet means this.

terms.definition: The leaves that appear after the rounded seed leaves and actually look like the adult plant.
terms.why: 'Thin once seedlings have their first true leaves' is the standard cue for thinning and potting on.

terms.definition: A crop that needs warm soil and warm nights and dies at the first frost — tomatoes, peppers, beans, cucumbers, squash.
terms.why: These wait until after your last frost, and rushing them into cold soil gains you nothing.
